I now have enough material from the fetched and searched pages to compile thorough verse-by-verse notes. Let me organize everything.

---

# Proverbs 1 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 – The proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel

**Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew word translated "proverbs" is *mashal*, which fundamentally means a comparison or similitude — something "set beside" something else for comparison. It covers a wider range than English "proverb": maxims, aphorisms, wise counsels, even parabolic discourses (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes that *mashal* derives from the verb meaning "to make like" or "to assimilate," and also "to have dominion," so proverbs carry both a comparative and an authoritative weight. Most modern commentators regard Solomon as the dominant spirit behind the collection, though some sayings of other wise men may be incorporated. "King of Israel" attaches to Solomon, not David.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/1.htm (see Proverbs 1:1 entry)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Gill (Baptist):** Emphasises that Solomon was an eminent type of Christ, who also spoke in proverbs (John 16:25). The titles "son of David, king of Israel" belong also to the Messiah, Solomon's antitype.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm

**Reformed/Evangelical (Guzik, Precept Austin):** Notes that Proverbs teach wisdom through short, memorable statements and are not to be treated as "laws" or universal promises. "Proverbs by design lays out pointed observations, meant to be memorized and pondered, not always intended to be applied 'across the board' to every situation without qualification" (Phillips, cited by Guzik). Kidner adds: "Naturally [proverbs] generalize, as a proverb must, and may therefore be charged with making life too tidy to be true."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary

**Modern Scholarship:** Proverbs belongs to a genre of wisdom literature common in the ancient Near East, with parallels in Egyptian works (e.g., *Teaching of Amenemope*) and Babylonian texts. There is debate whether Proverbs borrowed from or influenced these. Kidner says: "If Proverbs is the borrower here, the borrowing is not slavish but free and creative. Egyptian jewels, as at the Exodus, have been re-set to their advantage by Israelite workmen."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 2 – for gaining wisdom and discipline, for comprehending words of insight

**Traditional Reading:** The purpose clause begins. "Wisdom" (*chokhmah*) originally meant "firmness" or "solidity" — having convictions based on sound reasons, the opposite of being "carried about with every wind of doctrine" (Ellicott). "Instruction" (*mûsār*) is better rendered "discipline" — the knowledge of self-control. Gill says "wisdom" refers to the theory of truth and "instruction" to learning and putting it into practice. Precept Austin adds that *mûsār* often refers to child-training (discipline).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary

**Guzik:** Emphasises the difference between wisdom and knowledge: "Knowledge is the collection of facts; wisdom is the right use of what we know for daily living. Knowledge can tell one how financial systems work; wisdom manages a budget properly."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Reformed (Ligonier/Sproul):** "A person can have unbounded knowledge and not have wisdom. But the reverse is not the case; no one can have wisdom if he does not have knowledge." Wisdom cannot exist without knowledge, but knowledge alone is not wisdom.

- https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/wisdom-and-knowledge

---

## v. 3 – and for receiving instruction in wise living and in righteousness, justice, and equity

**Traditional Reading:** The Pulpit Commentary distinguishes: "justice" pertains to God, the supreme Judge and His eternal order; "judgment" (or "right") refers to established custom and law among men; "equity" (literally "what is straight") points to straightforward, honourable conduct (Pulpit Homiletics). Ellicott renders the phrase "the instruction of wisdom" as the discipline that results in *prudence* (*haskēl*) or practical wisdom — as David "behaved himself wisely" (1 Samuel 18:5). Precept Austin (Bob Utley) notes that "wise behavior" comes from the verb "to be successful" and that wisdom issues in godly behaviour.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/1.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary

---

## v. 4 – To impart prudence to the simple and knowledge and discretion to the young

**Traditional Reading:** The "simple" (Hebrew *pethi*) are literally "open ones" — those who, through inexperience, are open to every impression, good or bad. They are gullible, not necessarily fools (Pulpit). Ellicott says they are "open to good impressions and influences, but who also can be easily led astray." The Hebrew for "young man" (*na'ar*) can refer to any age from infancy to about twenty. "Discretion" (*m'zimmah*) is better rendered "thoughtfulness" — the habit of reflecting with attention and forethought upon life (Pulpit). Guzik adds that the simple man "is gullible, he is naïve. He may have opinions, but he lacks deeply thought-through and field-tested convictions" (citing Phillips).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Waltke (Evangelical/Reformed, cited by Guzik):** "The son and the gullible stand on the threshold of full adulthood. The time is at hand when the son and the gullible must make a decisive stand for the godly parents' and sages' world-and-life views and values. Two conflicting worldviews make their appeal, 'of Wisdom/Folly, Good/Pseudo-Good, Life/Death,' and one must choose between them, for there is no third way."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 5 – let the wise listen and gain instruction, and the discerning acquire wise counsel

**Traditional Reading:** Proverbs is not only for the simple and young; even the wise can grow through its teachings. Ellicott notes "wise counsels" is literally "arts of seamanship" — i.e., guiding oneself and others aright through the "waves of this troublesome world." The Pulpit Commentary says: "The wise man may listen and gain instruction; for men 'grow old, learning something fresh each day.' … Knowledge is practically infinite; we can think of no bounds to it."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/1.htm

**Gill (Baptist):** A man of spiritual understanding, through this book, "is fit to be a counsellor of others in things human and divine; in things moral, civil, and spiritual: he is fit to be in the cabinet council of princes."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 6 – by understanding the proverbs and parables, the sayings and riddles of the wise

**Traditional Reading:** "Dark sayings" (BSB: "riddles") is literally "knots" — intricate sayings like Samson's riddle (Judges 14:12) (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary says figurative or parabolic speech "half reveals and half conceals the soul within, and thus excites the curiosity, fixes the attention, stimulates exertion of thought in the listener. The best preachers leave much for the hearers to fill up for themselves."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 7 – The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline

**Traditional Reading — The Keynote Verse:** This is widely regarded as the motto or theme of the entire book. The "fear of the LORD" is not servile terror but reverential awe, "that affectionate reverence by which the child of God bends himself humbly and carefully to his Father's law" (Charles Bridges, cited in Precept Austin). Kidner calls it "a worshipping submission to the God of the covenant." Waltke says: "What the alphabet is to reading, notes to reading music, and numerals to mathematics, the fear of the LORD is to attaining the revealed knowledge of this book." The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew *reshith* ("beginning") has been understood three ways: (1) the initial step, the starting point; (2) the chief or most excellent part; (3) the origin or basis. The first sense is generally preferred. The "fear of the LORD" occurs thirteen times in Proverbs.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/1.htm (see Proverbs 1:7)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary

**Fools:** The Hebrew *'evîlîm* denotes "self-willed, headstrong persons, who will listen to no advice" (Ellicott). Gill says they are "incorrigible" and "unwilling to know God." Not intellectual deficiency but willful, moral rejection of God is in view.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm

**Reformed (Ligonier/R.C. Sproul):** Emphasises that "fear" is "filial fear" — as Martin Luther said, "the fear of a child who is in awe of his father and doesn't want to do anything that would violate his father and disrupt their loving relationship." It is reverence, awe, and respect. Sproul adds: "The fool is the person who has no reverence for God, and when you have no reverence for God, inevitably your life will show it." Wisdom is also inseparable from righteousness: "We cannot be wise without holiness, and we cannot be holy if we do not seek after wisdom."

- https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/wisdom-and-knowledge
- https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/proverbs

**Gill (Baptist):** Distinguishes between "servile fear" (fear of punishment) and "filial fear" which "supposes knowledge of God as a father, of his love and grace in Christ, particularly of his forgiving love." He says this fear "includes the whole of religious worship, both internal and external" and "this is the first and chief thing in spiritual and evangelical knowledge."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm

**Ellicott (Anglican):** Adds a notable New Testament perspective: the fear of the Lord was the beginning under the Old Covenant, given amid "blackness, and darkness, and tempest." But under the New Covenant, the higher duty of "love" supersedes — though fear remains the starting point. "He that feareth is not made perfect in love" (1 John 4:18). Yet the principle remains true that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** Guzik's treatment is largely in line with the traditional reading; he cites Bridges, Kidner, Ross, Clarke, Waltke, and Morgan. No distinctly Pentecostal distinctive emerges on this verse beyond the shared evangelical understanding.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 8 – Listen, my son, to your father's instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother

**Traditional Reading:** After establishing the fear of the LORD as the foundation, the next exhortation turns to the home — obedience to parents. This follows the order of the Decalogue: first table (duty to God), then second table beginning with "honour thy father and thy mother" (Gill). "My son" is the address of a master to a pupil; it occurs only twice more in Proverbs outside the first nine chapters (Ellicott). Both father and mother are mentioned, showing both parents share the responsibility of teaching wisdom. The word "law" (*torah*) here means teaching or direction, not the Mosaic law.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

**Guzik:** Notes the irony that Solomon, who had 700 wives and 300 concubines, left record of only one son, Rehoboam — and he was a fool. He also notes that "instruction" shows children are to be taught through words and reasoning, not only bodily punishment.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 9 – For they are a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck

**Traditional Reading:** Parental instruction, when received, adorns a child's life like a beautiful crown or necklace. Gill says: "The instructions and laws of parents being attended unto and obeyed by children, render them more lovely and amiable than any beautiful ornament whatever." Ellicott compares the "chains about thy neck" to the rewards given to Joseph (Genesis 41:42) and Daniel (Daniel 5:29). The imagery would be pleasing and attractive to young people.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 10 – My son, if sinners entice you, do not yield to them

**Traditional Reading:** The first specific warning in Proverbs concerns bad company. "Sinners" here means notorious, hardened sinners — those whose trade and constant course of life is sin (Gill). Guzik notes: "Significantly, this first instruction and warning in the book of Proverbs speaks to the company we keep and the friendships we make. There are few more powerful forces and influences upon our life than the friends we choose." Clarke (cited by Guzik) says: "They can do thee no harm unless thy will join in with them…. Not even the devil himself can lead a man into sin till he consents."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Ellicott:** Notes the historical context: brigandage was a constant danger in Palestine due to its wild terrain and proximity to predatory tribes, especially when government was weak.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 11 – If they say, "Come along, let us lie in wait for blood, let us ambush the innocent without cause"

**Traditional Reading:** Gill notes that the enticement is to leave one's proper place and join a violent gang. "Let us lay wait for blood" — the same Hebrew word can signify both "blood" and "money," since the one is sought for the sake of the other. "Without cause" means the victim is innocent and has done nothing to provoke the attack; the gang does it "freely" for themselves and with promised "impunity" (Gill). Ellicott takes "without cause" with "lurk" — though the victim has done them no harm.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

**Guzik:** Notes that Solomon describes the sinners' words in terms of their real meaning, not their actual phrasing. Gangs would appeal to riches and quick gain, not openly to bloodshed. "Solomon tells us to hear what people mean with such promises of quick and easy riches, not only what they say."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 12 – let us swallow them alive like Sheol, and whole like those descending into the Pit

**Traditional Reading:** "Sheol" is the grave or the underworld, and "the Pit" is synonymous — the place of the dead. The gang's violence is so total it is compared to death swallowing the living. Ellicott compares it to the fate of Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:30), who went down alive into the pit.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 13 – We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder

**Traditional Reading:** The enticement shifts to the promise of wealth. The violent gain is the gang's real motivation. Gill: young men are especially susceptible to the promise of quick riches.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 14 – Throw in your lot with us; let us all share one purse

**Traditional Reading:** The final enticement is the offer of belonging — "cast in thy lot among us." Garrett (cited by Guzik): "Apparently in ancient Israel, no less than in the modern world, the comradeship, easy money, and feeling of empowerment offered by gangs was a strong temptation to the young man." The "one purse" promises equality and shared wealth.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 15 – my son, do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path

**Traditional Reading:** The father's counsel is simple and absolute: stay away entirely. "Keep your foot from their path" — do not even begin to walk with them. The warning is preventative, not remedial.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 16 – For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood

**Traditional Reading:** The first reason given against joining them: the sheer evil of what they do. They are eager for wrongdoing — their feet "run" to it and they "make haste" to shed blood. Ellicott calls this "the horrible nature of the crime they are committing."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 17 – How futile it is to spread the net where any bird can see it!

**Traditional Reading:** This is a proverb within a proverb. The traditional interpretation (Ellicott, Guzik) is that even birds are wiser than these violent men — birds will not fly into a net spread in plain sight, yet the sinners cannot see that their own trap will catch them. God will bring punishment on them: in the "same net which they hid privily will their foot be taken" (Psalm 9:15) (Ellicott).

Garrett (cited by Guzik) offers a slightly different nuance: "The bird does not see any connection between the net and what is scattered on it; he just sees food that is free for the taking. In the process he is trapped and killed. In the same way, the gang cannot see the connection between their acts of robbery and the fate that entraps them."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 18 – But they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives

**Traditional Reading:** The great irony: the sinners think they are hunting the innocent (v. 11), but in reality they are hunting themselves. Divine justice turns the scheme back on the schemer. Ellicott: "They cannot see that in truth they are laying wait, not for the innocent, but for themselves, as God will deliver him, and bring the mischief they designed for him upon their own head."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 19 – Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors

**Traditional Reading:** The conclusion of the first discourse (Ellicott). Greed (*betsa'*, unjust gain) is self-destructive — it "takes away the life of its owners." The Hebrew idiom speaks of the greedy person as the "owner" of greed — the vice possesses him, and then destroys him. The same phrase "so are the ways" occurs in Job 8:13.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

**Guzik:** Notes the tragic irony that Solomon himself later fell into this trap through his wives who turned him to idolatry.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 20 – Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square

**Traditional Reading — Wisdom Personified:** The form *chokhmoth* (a plural or intensive form of *chokhmah*) signifies "the multiform excellences of wisdom" (Ellicott). Wisdom is personified as a woman crying out publicly — a poetic device. Ellicott says it is possible Solomon originally meant only to describe, in poetic language, the influence of those in whom the fear of the LORD dwells. Guzik: "Her cry is aloud but often ignored."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Christological Reading (Ellicott, citing Church Fathers):** From the earliest Christian times, this passage has been read as a prophecy of Christ. Ellicott notes that Luke 11:49 ("Therefore also said the wisdom of God, Behold, I send…") compared with Matthew 23:34 (where Jesus says "Behold, I send") suggests Jesus applied the title "Wisdom of God" to Himself. Paul calls Christ "the Wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), says He "has been made unto us wisdom" (1:30), and that in Him "are hid all the treasures of wisdom" (Colossians 2:3). The Fathers universally interpreted Wisdom in Proverbs 1, 8, and 9 as declaratory of Christ's work as Creator and Redeemer.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

**Poole (cited by Guzik):** "And this wisdom is said to cry with a loud voice, to intimate both God's earnestness in inviting sinners to repentance, and their inexcusableness if they do not hear such loud cries."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 21 – in the main concourse she cries aloud, at the city gates she makes her speech

**Traditional Reading:** Wisdom presents herself in every public place — streets, squares, concourses, gates. Kidner (cited by Guzik): "Here the open proclamation…to make it clear that the offer of wisdom is to the man in the street, and for the business of living, not to an élite for the pursuit of scholarship." The city gate was the place of judgment, commerce, and public assembly. Wisdom is available to all.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Ellicott:** "She cannot bear to see sinners rushing madly on their doom" — comparing Christ's weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 22 – "How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways? How long will scoffers delight in their scorn and fools hate knowledge?"

**Traditional Reading:** Three classes of persons are addressed (Ellicott, Guzik):

1. **Simple ones** (*pethi*): open to good or evil, but here shown to "love" their simplicity — they prefer their foolish ignorance to the effort of wisdom.
2. **Scorners** (*lētsîm*): proud, arrogant mockers who despise what is holy and pride themselves on cleverness. This class first appears in Solomon's prosperous era, favoured by religious indifference and scepticism (Ellicott). Wiersbe (cited by Guzik): "While the simple one has a blank look on his face, the scorner wears a sneer."
3. **Fools** (*khesîlîm*): dull, stupid, stolidly confident in their own wisdom — "people who are ignorant of truth because they're dull and stubborn" (Wiersbe).

Guzik notes a downward progression: "You started gullible, then became a fool, and ended up a scorner (mocker)."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 23 – If you had repented at my rebuke, then surely I would have poured out my spirit on you; I would have made my words known to you

**Traditional Reading:** This is an invitation to repent ("turn at my rebuke"). The promise is that Wisdom will "pour out my spirit" — traditionally understood as the spirit or mind of wisdom, making her words known. Ellicott connects this with Joel 2:28, promised by Christ (John 7:38-39), and fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Guzik says: "It seems that the description here is of the spirit of wisdom, not specifically the Holy Spirit. The two concepts do not contradict each other, but they are also not exactly the same."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

**Pentecostal/Charismatic reading:** While not finding a distinctly Pentecostal commentary on this verse in the sources searched, the language of "pour out my spirit" is naturally connected by Pentecostal readers with the Holy Spirit and the promise of empowerment. However, the sources reviewed (Enduring Word, preceptaustin.org) do not press a distinctly charismatic reading here beyond noting the connection.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 24 – Because you refused my call, and no one took my outstretched hand

**Traditional Reading:** Wisdom's tone shifts from mercy to judgment (cf. Psalm 101:1). The image of the outstretched hand recalls Romans 10:21: "All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people" (Ellicott). The rejection is personal and active — "you refused" and "no one regarded."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

---

## v. 25 – because you neglected all my counsel, and wanted none of my correction

**Traditional Reading:** The rejection is total — "all my counsel" and "none of my correction." The language is comprehensive and emphatic. This describes not mere neglect but active, willful dismissal.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 26 – in turn I will mock your calamity; I will sneer when terror strikes you

**Traditional Reading:** This is one of the most theologically challenging verses. Commentators are careful: Ellicott says of the similar expressions in Psalm 2:4, 37:13, and 59:8, "They are not to be taken literally, of course, for the sight of human folly can give no pleasure to Him. They signify that He will act as if He mocked when He refuses to hear their cry." Guzik, citing Waltke, says: "Wisdom does not laugh at disaster, but at the triumph of what is right over what is wrong when your disaster happens." The point is that rejected wisdom has nothing to offer the fool when judgment falls.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 27 – when your dread comes like a storm, and your destruction like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish overwhelm you

**Traditional Reading:** The imagery of sudden, overwhelming judgment — a storm, a whirlwind. The language is poetic and vivid. Distress and anguish come together as an unstoppable force. Guzik: "Rejected wisdom has nothing to offer the fool when destruction comes like a whirlwind."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 28 – Then they will call on me, but I will not answer; they will earnestly seek me, but will not find me

**Traditional Reading:** When calamity strikes, the fools finally call on Wisdom — but it is too late. This is not about God's unwillingness to forgive the repentant, but about the nature of wisdom: it cannot be summoned at will in a crisis after a lifetime of rejection. Guzik: "Those who reject wisdom's repeated calls cannot demand her help in crisis; when trouble comes, they will call but she will not answer."

A comparison to Proverbs 1:28 being about a point of no return — "because wisdom has been continually rejected, wisdom will laugh at the calamity of those who have rejected it" (Ross, cited by Guzik).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 29 – For they hated knowledge and chose not to fear the LORD

**Traditional Reading:** The root cause of their ruin is stated: they "hated knowledge" and "chose not to fear the LORD." This echoes verse 7. Their destruction is not arbitrary — it flows from their own choices. The verb "chose" indicates a deliberate act of the will.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 30 – They accepted none of my counsel; they despised all my reproof

**Traditional Reading:** This restates the comprehensive rejection described in v. 25, reinforcing the justice of the judgment. The parallelism of "none" and "all" emphasises totality.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 31 – So they will eat the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices

**Traditional Reading:** The principle of sowing and reaping. They will "eat the fruit" — the consequences are organic to their choices. "Be filled to the full with their own fancies" (or "devices") — they get exactly what they chose. The judgment is not external but the natural outworking of their own path. This is the "poetic justice" of wisdom literature.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 32 – For the waywardness of the simple will slay them, and the complacency of fools will destroy them

**Traditional Reading:** Two fatal errors are identified: the "waywardness" (or "turning away") of the simple — their refusal to turn to wisdom — and the "complacency" (or "careless ease," "security") of fools — their false sense of safety. Precept Austin (Bob Utley) observes that this verse and v. 33 present the "two ways" (cursing and blessing) pattern seen in Deuteronomy 30 and Psalm 1.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

---

## v. 33 – But whoever listens to me will dwell in safety, secure from the fear of evil

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter closes with a promise. The one who listens to Wisdom will "dwell safely" (*shakan betach*) — live in security, at ease, without dread of evil. This is not a promise of a trouble-free life but of ultimate spiritual security — "secure from the fear of evil." Gill says this is a promise of "safety and rest to those that hearken to her." The contrast with v. 32 is stark: destruction for fools, security for the wise.

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences Found

### Christological Interpretation of Wisdom (vv. 20–33)

The early Church Fathers universally interpreted Wisdom personified in Proverbs 1, 8, and 9 as referring to Christ, the eternal Wisdom of God (Ellicott). This reading is preserved in both **Catholic** and **Orthodox** traditions, as well as in classic **Anglican** and **Reformed** interpretation. However, Evangelical commentators (including Guzik at Enduring Word, and the Precept Austin compilers) tend to read the personification more as a literary device, while still acknowledging the typological connection to Christ. No Catholic or Orthodox specific pages were located in the searches to provide direct citation.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm

### The "Fear of the LORD" (v. 7)

While all traditions agree that "fear" means reverential awe, not terror, nuances differ:

- **Reformed (Ligonier/Sproul):** Emphasises "filial fear" (Luther's term) and insists that wisdom cannot exist without also pursuing knowledge. Rejects anti-intellectual piety. Wisdom is inseparable from righteousness.
- **Baptist (Gill):** Emphasises the experiential knowledge of God as Father through Christ and ties fear to the whole of religious worship.
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Notes the progression from Old Covenant fear to New Covenant love, seeing fear as the necessary starting point that love fulfills.
- **Lutheran (Lange, via StudyLight):** "The fear of Jehovah is the beginning of knowledge; wisdom and discipline fools despise" — rendered straightforwardly, emphasising the antithetical parallelism.

- https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/wisdom-and-knowledge
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/1.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/1.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/proverbs-1.html (Lange)

### Proverbs as Promises vs. General Principles

A significant modern Evangelical debate concerns whether proverbs are guarantees. **John MacArthur** (Baptist/Reformed, cited by Precept Austin) states clearly: "Proverbs are divine guidelines and wise observations, i.e., teaching underlying principles which are not always inflexible laws or absolute promises." **Guzik** agrees, noting proverbs "should not be regarded as 'laws' or even universal promises." This stands in contrast to **Prosperity/Word of Faith** teaching (not directly found in the searched sources for this chapter, but relevant as general background), which sometimes treats proverbial statements as unconditional promises for material blessing. No specific prosperity-teaching source on Proverbs 1 was located.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-1-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-1/

### "Pour Out My Spirit" (v. 23)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Connects directly to Joel 2:28 and Pentecost (Acts 2:17) — a prophetic anticipation of the Holy Spirit.
- **Guzik (Charismatic/Evangelical):** Cautious — says it describes "the spirit of wisdom, not specifically the Holy Spirit," while noting the two concepts do not contradict.
- No distinctly **Pentecostal** source was located in the searches for this specific verse.

### "I Will Laugh at Your Calamity" (v. 26)

All traditions found agree this is anthropopathic language — describing God acting *as if* He mocks, not that He literally takes pleasure in suffering. The agreement is broad across sources (Ellicott, Guzik/Waltke, Gill).
